content: Uranium dioxide (UO2) and triuranium octoxide (U3O8) are both solid uranium oxides that exhibit low solubility in water and remain relatively stable across a wide range of environmental conditions. Among these, U3O8 is considered the most stable uranium compound under typical conditions and is the form most commonly found in nature. In contrast, UO2 is the primary form of uranium used as nuclear reactor fuel. Over time, at ambient temperatures, UO2 will gradually oxidize to form U3O8. Due to their chemical stability, uranium oxides are generally regarded as the preferred forms for long-term storage or disposal of uranium. In aqueous chemistry, uranium exists in four primary oxidation states, represented by the ions U³⁺ (red), U⁴⁺ (green), UO₂⁺ (unstable), and UO₂²⁺ (yellow). While some solid and semi-metallic compounds, such as uranium monoxide (UO) and uranium sulfide (US), exist in the formal oxidation state of uranium(II), no simple uranium(II) ions are known to exist in solution. The U³⁺ ion is highly unstable, as it reacts with water to release hydrogen gas. The UO₂²⁺ ion, representing uranium(VI), forms compounds such as carbonates, chlorides, and sulfates, and it also forms complexes with various organic chelating agents, the most common being uranyl acetate. The interaction of carbonate anions with uranium(VI) significantly alters the Pourbaix diagram when the medium is changed from water to a carbonate-containing solution. While most carbonates are insoluble in water, uranium carbonates are often water-soluble. This is because the uranium(VI) cation can bind two terminal oxides and three or more carbonate anions to form anionic complexes. Fraction diagrams illustrate that as the pH of a uranium(VI) solution increases, uranium transitions to hydrated uranium oxide hydroxide and, at higher pH levels, to anionic hydroxide complexes. When carbonate is introduced, uranium forms a series of carbonate complexes as the pH increases, which enhances uranium solubility in the pH range of 6 to 8. This behavior is critical when considering the long-term stability of spent uranium dioxide nuclear fuels. Uranium metal reacts with hydrogen at temperatures between 250°C and 300°C to form uranium hydride. At even higher temperatures, the hydrogen can be reversibly removed, making uranium hydrides useful as starting materials for producing reactive uranium powders and various uranium carbide, nitride, and halide compounds. Uranium hydride exists in two crystalline forms: the α-form, obtained at lower temperatures, and the β-form, formed above 250°C. Uranium carbides, such as uranium monocarbide (UC), uranium dicarbide (UC₂), and diuranium tricarbide (U₂C₃), are relatively inert semimetallic compounds that are minimally soluble in acids, react with water, and can ignite in air to form U₃O₈. UC and UC₂ are produced by adding carbon to molten uranium or exposing uranium to carbon monoxide at high temperatures. U₂C₃, stable below 1800°C, is prepared by subjecting a heated mixture of UC and UC₂ to mechanical stress. Uranium nitrides, such as uranium mononitride (UN), uranium dinitride (UN₂), and diuranium trinitride (U₂N₃), are formed by directly exposing uranium metal to nitrogen. All uranium fluorides are derived from uranium tetrafluoride (UF₄), which is prepared by hydrofluorination of uranium dioxide. Reduction of UF₄ with hydrogen at 1000°C produces uranium trifluoride (UF₃). UF₆ is prepared from uranium dioxide and uranium hydride through a two-step process involving hydrofluorination and fluorination. The resulting UF₆ is a highly reactive white solid that sublimates easily and is the most volatile uranium compound known. Uranium tetrachloride (UCl₄) can be prepared by directly combining chlorine with uranium metal or uranium hydride. Reduction of UCl₄ with hydrogen produces uranium trichloride (UCl₃), while higher uranium chlorides are formed by reacting UCl₄ with additional chlorine. All uranium chlorides react with water and air. Bromides and iodides of uranium, such as UBr₃, UBr₄, UI₃, and UI₄, are formed by direct reaction of uranium with bromine or iodine or by adding uranium hydride (UH₃) to the respective acids. Uranium oxyhalides, including UO₂F₂, UOCl₂, UO₂Cl₂, and UO₂Br₂, are water-soluble, with their stability decreasing as the atomic weight of the halide increases. Naturally occurring uranium consists of three major isotopes: uranium-238 (99.28% abundance), uranium-235 (0.71%), and uranium-234 (0.0054%). All three isotopes are radioactive, with uranium-238 being the most abundant and stable, having a half-life of 4.51 billion years. Uranium-235 has a half-life of 713 million years, and uranium-234 has a half-life of 248,000 years. Uranium-238 undergoes alpha decay through an 18-member decay series, ultimately forming lead-206. Uranium-235, also known as actino-uranium, decays through a 15-member series ending in lead-207, with intermediate isotopes such as protactinium-231 and actinium-227. The consistent decay rates in these series make parent-to-daughter element ratios useful for radiometric dating. Uranium-233 is produced from thorium-232 via neutron bombardment. Uranium-235 is critical for nuclear reactors and weapons because it is the only naturally occurring fissile isotope, capable of sustaining a chain reaction with thermal neutrons. Uranium-238 is also significant because it absorbs neutrons to produce plutonium-239, another fissile isotope. Enrichment of uranium ore through isotope separation is necessary to concentrate uranium-235 for use in nuclear weapons and most nuclear power plants, except for pressurized heavy water reactors. A majority of neutrons released by fissioning uranium-235 must impact other uranium-235 atoms to sustain the nuclear chain reaction. The concentration of uranium-235 required to achieve this is referred to as the critical mass. Enriched uranium typically contains 3-5% uranium-235. The enrichment process produces large quantities of uranium depleted in uranium-235, with a corresponding increase in uranium-238, known as depleted uranium (DU).
